subtopic: A promotion and the ego that follows
passage:
Skip-level check-in notes. Written by Mohit, engineering manager.
Sudha (25) has been on the billing team for three years. Since Harish, her former desk-mate, became team lead in April, the team's stand-ups have got shorter and quieter. I asked Sudha why.
She took a while. 'He doesn't come to our lunch table any more. Fine, he's busy. But when I raised the tax rounding issue in May, he said, "I've already decided that." So now I think twice. Three times. Mostly I don't say it.'
She told me, almost as an aside, that she had spotted a second rounding problem two weeks ago and kept it to herself. It surfaced yesterday in a customer complaint.
'I used to be the one who asked the annoying questions,' she said. 'I miss that version of me.'
Next step: speak to Harish about how the team is experiencing him, and set up an open issue list anyone can add to.

qa.q: When did Sudha first raise the tax rounding issue?
qa.a: She raised the tax rounding issue in May.

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling when she kept the second rounding problem to herself?
qa.a: She felt dropped by her old desk-mate and unsure her ideas were welcome, so speaking up no longer felt worth the risk.

qa.q: What turning point can Mohit create at this stage?
qa.a: By telling Harish how the team is experiencing him and opening an issue list anyone can add to, Mohit can make it safe to raise problems again.

qa.q: How might Harish be affected by the team's silence, even if he hasn't noticed it?
qa.a: Harish is losing early warnings like the rounding problem, so the team looks calm to him while hidden issues grow.

grounding: It shows a former teammate who feels dropped by the new lead, stops offering ideas, and lets a problem stay hidden, making the team quieter.

subtopic: A promotion and the ego that follows
passage:
Tuesday
Aparna and I sat next to each other for two years. We shared earphones, lunch boxes, the lot. Since she became lead she eats with the managers and replies to my messages with one word. 'Noted.' 'Ok.' I know she's busy. It still stings.
Today in the planning call she set the launch for the 20th. I know the payment tests won't be ready by then. I typed a message to her in the chat: 'Can we talk about the 20th? I'm worried about testing.' I looked at it for a long time. Then I deleted it.
What if she thinks I'm being difficult because I'm jealous? Or that I'm trying to show her up?
After the call, Faiz messaged me privately: 'Is the 20th realistic??' So he sees it too. Neither of us said anything in the call.
The whole team was so quiet today.
— Rukmini

qa.q: What launch date did Aparna set in the planning call?
qa.a: She set the launch for the 20th.

qa.q: What was Rukmini worried about when deleting the message?
qa.a: Rukmini worried that Aparna would think the concern came from jealousy or from wanting to show her up.

qa.q: What small step could Rukmini try instead of staying silent?
qa.a: Rukmini could raise the testing concern with Faiz together, as a plain fact about the payment tests, so it feels less personal.

qa.q: How might Aparna be affected if nobody raises the testing problem?
qa.a: Aparna could walk into a failed launch on the 20th without knowing her own team had seen it coming.

grounding: It shows a former teammate who feels dropped by the new lead and second-guesses speaking up, so a real problem stays hidden and the team goes quiet.

subtopic: A promotion and the ego that follows
passage:
Seema, you know what's strange? I used to be the loudest person in our team meetings. Now I just nod. Since Kunal became our lead, he eats lunch with the other managers, answers my messages with one word, and last month he said, "Let's keep ideas to the agenda, Madhuri," in front of everyone. I felt like a schoolgirl.
So I stopped. Two weeks ago I noticed the vendor's figures didn't match ours. Old me would have raised it in the meeting. New me thought, why bother, he'll just think I'm showing off. I told nobody.
It blew up on Friday. The client caught it. Kunal was furious and asked why nobody had flagged it. I sat there with my face hot. I had flagged it, in my head.
The whole team has gone quiet like that. It's not a stronger team, Seema. It's just a quieter one.

qa.q: What did Madhuri notice two weeks ago?
qa.a: The vendor's figures didn't match ours.

qa.q: What was Madhuri feeling when Kunal asked why nobody had flagged it?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and conflicted, her face hot, knowing she had seen the problem but had stopped speaking up after feeling dropped.

qa.q: What turning point is available to the team now?
qa.a: Madhuri could tell Kunal privately that people have stopped raising issues since his manner changed, and share what she saw in the figures.

qa.q: How might Kunal experience the team's silence?
qa.a: Kunal may feel let down and blindsided, not realising his own distance is why problems no longer reach him.

grounding: A former teammate feels dropped by the new lead, stops offering ideas, and a hidden problem surfaces too late in a quieter team.

subtopic: A promotion and the ego that follows
passage:
Week 1. Dhruv, who had sat beside Mridul for three years, was made lead. Mridul bought sweets for the whole floor and hugged him. That evening Dhruv moved into the cabin by the window.
Week 3. Mridul suggested a faster way to run the monthly report. Dhruv said, "Let me think about it," and never mentioned it again. The Friday chai they used to share now happened without Mridul; through the glass he saw Dhruv laughing with the other leads.
Week 6. In the Monday meeting, Mridul noticed that the testing plan skipped the older phones most of their customers used. He opened his mouth, then closed it. Would Dhruv even listen? Would it sound like sulking? He said nothing. Two others stared at their laptops too. The meeting ended in eleven minutes, the quietest they had ever had.

qa.q: What did Mridul notice the testing plan skipped?
qa.a: The older phones most of their customers used.

qa.q: What was Mridul feeling when he closed his mouth in the Monday meeting?
qa.a: He felt hurt and unsure, second-guessing whether Dhruv would listen or see his point as sulking.

qa.q: What could change things at this stage?
qa.a: Mridul could raise the testing gap with Dhruv one-to-one and mention that the team has gone quiet, giving Dhruv a chance to reconnect.

qa.q: What might Dhruv be missing in the short, quiet meeting?
qa.a: Dhruv may think the quiet means agreement, missing that his distance has cost him the team's warnings, like the older-phones gap.

grounding: Over six weeks a former teammate feels dropped by the new lead and stops offering ideas, leaving the team quieter and a problem unspoken.

subtopic: A promotion and the ego that follows
passage:
Jaya, you say your old batchmate is now your manager and you've stopped talking in meetings. Let me tell you about the year my friend Kamala became head clerk at the post office where we both worked. We had shared tiffin every day for five years.
The week she was promoted, she began eating at the superintendent's table. When I pointed out a mistake in the money-order register, she said, "I'll decide what's a mistake now, Pallavi." I went home and cried into my pillow, silly girl that I was.
After that, I kept my mouth shut. So did the others. When the register didn't tally in March, all six of us had seen it coming. Not one of us said a word. Kamala faced the inquiry alone, and we sat at our desks feeling guilty and, I'm ashamed to say, a little glad.
That silence cost all of us something. Think about that before you swallow your next idea.

qa.q: How long had Pallavi and Kamala shared tiffin?
qa.a: Every day for five years.

qa.q: What did young Pallavi feel after Kamala's remark about deciding mistakes?
qa.a: She felt hurt and dropped by her old friend, enough to cry into her pillow and stop speaking up.

qa.q: What choice inside the story made the March problem worse?
qa.a: Pallavi and the others chose silence after feeling dropped, so no one flagged the register before it failed to tally.

qa.q: How might Kamala have felt facing the inquiry alone?
qa.a: Kamala probably felt shocked and isolated, realising the colleagues who once warned her had stopped speaking up.

grounding: An elder recalls feeling dropped by a promoted friend, going silent with the others, and how that silence hid a problem from the new head.

subtopic: A promotion and the ego that follows
passage: The release was due at nine the next morning, and at seven in the evening the payment screen still froze on older phones. Ira noticed it first. Two months ago she would have rolled her chair over to Anirban's desk and said, "Look at this, it's weird." Now Anirban sat in the glass cabin by the window, and the last two times she had raised something in the stand-up he had cut her off with "Let's take that offline" and never come back to it. She opened a message to him, wrote "Small thing on payments," and stopped. The office lights clicked to night mode. Beside her, Farhan was quietly patching around the same bug without telling anyone. "Should we flag it?" Ira whispered. Farhan shrugged. "He'll say we're slowing things down." They both kept typing, and the message stayed unsent.

qa.q: What was due at nine the next morning?
qa.a: The release was due at nine the next morning.

qa.q: Why does Ira stop before sending the message to Anirban?
qa.a: She feels hurt and unsure of her place, because the last two times she raised something he cut her off and never came back to it.

qa.q: What turning point is available here, and who could take it?
qa.a: Ira could still send the message, framed as a risk to the release; Anirban could make it safe by asking the team directly what is worrying them before a launch.

qa.q: What is Anirban likely missing from inside the glass cabin?
qa.a: He probably thinks the team is fine because it is quiet, while a real bug is being hidden from him and fixed in secret.

grounding: Shows former teammates feeling dropped by a newly promoted lead and holding back a problem, which leaves the lead uninformed.
